title: bug: preview and release disagree on which installed policy is effective, so a newer policy without opt-ins cannot disable automatic approval

A test installs an older opted-in EVALUATION policy, then installs a newer one declaring no opt-ins, and asserts automatic preview approval is REFUSED with its stable code and layer. This is the reviewer's reproduction and it must go from red to green.

A test asserts preview and release select the SAME slice ref for the same store state, across at least the supersession case and the genuinely ambiguous two-declaring-slices case. Assert the ref, not merely that both allowed or both refused.
The ambiguity behaviour the current header defends is preserved: two declaring slices still refuse fail-closed, with the same code as today. Name the existing arm that proves it, or add one.
Non-vacuity: revert the selector to the historical-filter form and confirm the supersession arm goes red. Quote the red.
`pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` and `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test` both EXIT 0 with their `Test Files N passed (N)` count lines quoted.

implementationPlan.description: Implement the single shared selector `selectEffectiveAutoApprovalPolicy(store: SqliteEventStore, projectId: string): {readonly ref: string; readonly slice: JsonValue} | null` in new bootstrap/effective-auto-policy.ts, with a one-line .js runtime bridge exporting its .ts module. Add its focused real-store test cases in release-auto-decide.test.ts before implementation. Read installedSlices(stateOf(readDurableLedger(...), policyAggregateId(...))) once, then scan Object.entries in REVERSE INSTALL ORDER, never digest-sorted order. Ignore non-EVALUATION artifacts using existing sliceKindOf; for each encountered evaluation-like candidate require existing @moe/core derivePolicySliceDigest to succeed and equal its installed ref before treating its opt-ins as authority. An invalid candidate encountered in the current suffix or unreadable ledger returns null, never an older fallback. Stop at the FIRST valid empty-autoApprovalOptIns slice in the reverse scan: if no later declaration exists, return THIS RESET SLICE and ref; if one later declaring slice exists, return that slice; if >=2 exist, return null. With no reset, apply the same 0/1/>1 declaration rule (0 -> null). Declaration means a nonempty opt-in array, independent of gate action: filtering by preview/release action would create two effective policies again. Matching actions/tiers stays solely in the engine. Freeze the returned wrapper; write nothing and do not cache across calls. Canonical JSDoc HERE states the human reset/ambiguity rule once, cites installPolicy's immutable hex64 insertion order plus JSON preservation, explains reverse scan/last-reset semantics and validation. Tests cover empty state, artifacts not acting as resets, malformed evaluation-like bytes not clearing competing declarations, and unreadable store returning null; pin the caller's existing POLICY_UNRESOLVED code/layer when the caller is exercised. No new codes/layer constants, policy schema, event, command, active pointer, or manifest edit. Target <250 production lines.
implementationPlan.note:
Shared selector landed. `selectEffectiveAutoApprovalPolicy(store, projectId): {ref, slice} | null` in new apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/effective-auto-policy.ts (152 physical lines, well under the 250 target) + one-line .js runtime bridge `export * from "./effective-auto-policy.ts";`.

ALGORITHM as planned: read `installedSlices(stateOf(readDurableLedger(...), policyAggregateId(...)))` ONCE inside try/catch (throw -> null, never an older fallback), then `Object.entries` scanned by DESCENDING INDEX — reverse INSERTION order, never sorted, so nothing orders by content digest. Per candidate: non-EVALUATION per existing `sliceKindOf` is skipped as inert; an EVALUATION-shaped candidate whose `derivePolicySliceDigest` refuses or does not equal its installed ref returns null (fail closed in the current suffix); a non-array `autoApprovalOptIns` returns null. First valid EMPTY-opt-ins slice is the RESET BOUNDARY and ends the scan: `return declared ?? selected(ref, slice)` — the reset SLICE and ref when no newer declaration exists, the sole newer declaration when there is one. A second declaration with no reset between returns null. No reset anywhere applies the same 0/1/many rule to the whole history. Declaration = NONEMPTY opt-in array, action-INDEPENDENT: filtering by the caller's action would recreate two effective policies. Returned wrapper is Object.freeze'd; writes nothing; no cross-call cache (installed set re-read every call).

Reset returns its SLICE rather than null on purpose: the gate still composes against a policy the operator installed and core refuses with its own AUTO_APPROVAL_NOT_OPTED_IN under a named policyRevisionRef, instead of losing the ref to a selection-layer refusal. null is reserved for nothing-installed / nothing-declared / ambiguity / validity refusal.

Canonical JSDoc lives HERE and states the owner's 2026-09-11 ruling once (reset-then-ambiguity, with plain latest-wins and an active-policy pointer recorded as DECLINED), cites installPolicy's `{...current,[sliceRef]:slice}` hex64 insertion order + BOOTSTRAP_POLICY_SLICE_ALREADY_INSTALLED + the JSON round trip preserving it, and explains why a sorted scan is wrong.

FOCUSED REAL-STORE ARMS added to release-auto-decide.test.ts, new describe `selectEffectiveAutoApprovalPolicy is the ONE effective-policy rule` (9 arms): empty store -> null; sole declaration after the seed's opt-in-free tail (with the tail's emptiness asserted as a precondition); reset-supersedes -> the reset's own ref; re-arm after reset; two declarations -> null with a single-declaration positive control first; ambiguity CLEARED by the next reset then re-armed; non-EVALUATION artifact (non-hex ref) INERT; evaluation-LOOKALIKE bytes cannot pose as a reset; unreadable (closed) store -> null AND the caller pinned at RELEASE_AUTO_POLICY_UNRESOLVED @ RELEASE_AUTO_DECISION.

The lookalike arm asserts THE CASE WAS ACTUALLY GENERATED through the same production surfaces the selector uses: `sliceKindOf(ref, installed[ref])` is "EVALUATION" and `derivePolicySliceDigest(installed[ref]).ok` is false. Mechanism measured, not assumed: `validSlice` is exact-arity over {sliceRef,rules,autoApprovalOptIns}(+riskClassifications), so an extra `note` key makes the derivation refuse, and installPolicy only enforces the content address when `sliceDigest.ok`. The unreadable-store arm opens OUTSIDE the fixture registry (SqliteEventStore.openEphemeralForProjectTest) so afterEach `closeStores` cannot double-close it.

HUMAN RULING — the product decision this row blocked on is now ANSWERED. Authority, not a proposal.

The rule: an opt-in-free EVALUATION install is a RESET BOUNDARY. It clears older declarations for BOTH gates, so installing a policy that declares no opt-ins works as a kill switch on preview and release alike. After that reset boundary, if TWO OR MORE slices declare, both gates still refuse FAIL-CLOSED with today's existing code and layer. Ambiguity is preserved, not collapsed.

That is exactly the proposal architect-e29e1d0e recorded in comment-494c57b8 at 09:26:52 and correctly refused to implement without confirmation. It is now confirmed. Treat it as the adopted product rule and plan to it.

I put three options to the human and this was chosen deliberately over the other two, so do not re-litigate either:
- Newest-install-always-wins was REJECTED. It is simpler and matches release's current newestEvaluationSlice behaviour, but it makes ambiguity unreachable and therefore contradicts DoD 4, which requires the two-declaring fail-closed refusal be preserved with the same code as today. Choosing it would have meant striking DoD 4.
- Adding an explicit active-policy or supersedes field to the durable slice was REJECTED for this row. It is the cleaner model and may be worth its own row later, but it changes the slice schema and bootstrap-policy-services installPolicy, which is wider than this bug and conflicts with DoD 1's requirement that the rule live in one exported function both gates call rather than in a new durable field.

So the shape is unchanged from the row as written: one named exported selector implementing reset-boundary-then-ambiguity, called by both preview-auto-composition and release-auto-approval, with the grep in DoD 1 proving no second selector survives. The existing arms you already located are the anchors — preview-auto-decision.test.ts's 'declines when TWO installed slices both declare the preview gate's opt-in' asserting PREVIEW_AUTO_POLICY_UNRESOLVED @ PREVIEW_AUTO_DECISION for DoD 4, and release-auto-decide.test.ts's newest-opt-in-free reset arm asserting RELEASE_AUTO_NOT_ALLOWED @ CORE_REDUCER with AUTO_APPROVAL_NOT_OPTED_IN.

One thing the ruling does NOT settle, because nobody asked and you should not assume it: what happens when a reset boundary is followed by exactly ONE declaring slice, and then ANOTHER reset, and then one more declaring slice. The rule says the most recent reset boundary is the one that counts, so only declarations after the LAST reset compete. HUMAN RULING on the PRODUCT_DECISION_REQUIRED block. Put to the owner in the REPL by architect-bb193f43 on 2026-09-11 and answered directly by them. This is authority to implement, not a proposal.

THE RULE: NEWEST INSTALL RESETS, THEN AMBIGUITY STILL REFUSES.

  install A (declares opt-ins)        -> automatic approval ON, A governs
  install B (declares NO opt-ins)     -> automatic approval OFF; the reset clears A, which no
                                         longer counts as a competing declaration
  install C (declares opt-ins)        -> automatic approval ON, C governs
  C and D both declared after a reset -> REFUSE, PREVIEW_AUTO_POLICY_UNRESOLVED

So an opt-in-free install is how an operator turns automatic approval off, and it CLEARS older
declarations rather than sitting beside them. Only declarations made after the most recent reset
compete; when more than one competes the gate still refuses fail-closed with the code it uses today.

WHAT THE OWNER EXPLICITLY DID NOT CHOOSE, and why it matters when you plan:
- NOT plain latest-wins. That was offered and declined because it deletes the fail-closed refusal
  for the two-declaring case. The existing arm pinning PREVIEW_AUTO_POLICY_UNRESOLVED @
  PREVIEW_AUTO_DECISION stays, and DoD item 4 stays satisfiable as written.
- NOT an explicit active-policy pointer. That was offered and declined. Do NOT add a policy.activate
  command, a new event, or a schema field. The owner chose the option annotated "no schema change;
  selection rule reads install order", so the rule is derived from the existing immutable install
  history. bootstrap-policy-services.ts keeps recording immutable slices untouched.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SHARED SELECTOR: the same rule governs preview AND automatic release, so
release stops selecting simply "the newest EVALUATION" and adopts reset-then-compete too. DoD item
1's single-seam requirement and item 3's same-ref parity now have a definite rule to assert against.

The measurement in comment-494c57b8f55941358b8d7dbbe45e4ddf stands and is the starting point;
nothing in it is invalidated by this ruling. Re-measure the two selector line ranges at your own
claim HEAD before planning, since another row may have moved them.

comments.author: architect-bb193f43
comments.content:
PLANNING NOTE for whoever holds this row, from architect-bb193f43 at main 0c215e82. The owner's ruling (comment-4fdd31cf61ee4d49941e0255d16422fe) turns on INSTALL ORDER, so here is what I measured about whether install order is actually available. Re-measure before relying on it.

MEASURED - THE TWO SELECTORS ORDER THEIR REFS DIFFERENTLY, AND NEITHER READS THE EVENT SEQUENCE.

release/release-auto-approval.ts, newestEvaluationSlice: iterates `for (const ref of Object.keys(installed))` and keeps overwriting `selected`, so it takes the LAST key. That is OBJECT KEY INSERTION ORDER, and its own docstring calls it "the LAST digest-addressed installed EVALUATION slice".

preview/preview-auto-composition.ts, evaluationSliceOf: filters then calls `.sort()` on the refs. Refs are content DIGESTS, so that is lexicographic digest order, which carries no chronological meaning at all. It only works today because the code then requires exactly one survivor and discards the order.

So release leans on insertion order and preview leans on digest order. Neither reads the durable event sequence.

MEASURED - WHY INSERTION ORDER CURRENTLY TRACKS INSTALL ORDER. bootstrap-policy-services.ts builds the next state as `{ slices: { ...current, [sliceRef]: slice } }`, one install at a time, and refuses a repeat ref with BOOTSTRAP_POLICY_SLICE_ALREADY_INSTALLED. So the object is append-only and its key order is install order. It also emits `PolicyInstalled` with payload `{ sliceRef }`, which is the ORDERED, DURABLE record.

MY INFERENCE, NOT A MEASUREMENT, AND THE REASON I AM WRITING THIS: deriving "most recent reset" from JS object key order makes a load-bearing product rule depend on an incidental property of how the state object happens to be rebuilt. Any future change that reconstructs the slice map - a migration, a normalisation, a serialisation round trip that sorts keys, a fold that rebuilds from events in a different order - silently moves which policy governs, and no test that only asserts "exactly one survivor" would notice. The `PolicyInstalled` event sequence is the authority for chronology and it already exists.

SUGGESTION, not a constraint on your plan: have the shared selector fold the PolicyInstalled event sequence to find the newest EVALUATION slice declaring no preview opt-in (the reset), then take the declaring slices installed after it, then apply the ruling's refuse-on-more-than-one. If you instead rely on key order, add an arm that proves the rule survives a rebuild of the slice map, so the dependency is pinned rather than assumed.

This does not change the DoD. It bears on DoD item 1 (one seam both gates call) and item 3 (same-ref parity across supersession and ambiguity), because both need a definite chronological rule to assert against.
